newsitem.title: USA: Data coverage improving in emerging markets - study.
newsitem.headline: Data coverage improving in emerging markets - study.

text.p: Emerging markets are showing continued improvement in the area of data transparency, a development that promises to sustain private capital flows to these regions, the Institute of International Finance said on Thursday.

"We anticipate that there will increasingly be a virtuous circle in which countries seek to improve their data release practices to provide better information to capital markets and the markets reward them for doing so," IIF chief economist William Cline told reporters.

An IIF analysis of 28 emerging market economies showed that many countries improved their data reporting substantially in the year following the Mexican crisis and that some countries made further improvements last year.
The 28 economies reviewed in the report received approximately $250 billion in private capital inflows in 1996, the vast majority of all flows to developing countries.
The report examined the timeliness and comprehensiveness of data coverage in selected countries, but did not address the quality of the data.

Among the countries studied, Brazil, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Peru, Turkey and Taiwan were cited as attaining the highest performance against the Institute's benchmark standards for coverage and timeliness.
Those countries that made the greatest improvements in timeliness versus 1996 were Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Russian Federation and Taiwan.
Countries which the Institute said had "a long way to go" in meeting basic standards of data release included China, Egypt, Hong Kong, Kuwait, Morocco, Saudi Arabia and Tunisia.
"The broad picture is that there is improvement ... though there is not a uniform trend toward improvement," said Cline.
In many data categories, the levels of timely reporting were high, but Cline noted that certain areas of coverage were lacking.
From the standpoint of the international capital markets, the areas that remain of greatest concern include data on amortization profiles, short-term debt and fiscal performance, he said.
The report showed that only 65 percent of the countries studied reported data on amortization schedules and public sector borrowing requirements.

Charles Dallara, managing director at the IIF, stressed that the Institute's findings were not meant to represent country ratings of the kind produced by ratings agencies such as Standard & Poors and Moody's Investors Service.
"Data transparency alone is not going to assure an investor or lender of soundness," Dallara said.
Rather, the Institute termed the data transparency evaluations "only one part in the overall picture in evaluating a country."
